articles.body: In this article From exposed secrets to cloud compromiseFollow-on actionsMitigating application credential abuse activityDefending against agentic AI attacksMicrosoft detectionsAdvanced hunting queries Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization. Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. Additionally, Microsoft observed malicious activity originating from two IP addresses potentially associated with this campaign. We identified malicious operations from 65.87.223[.]26, including indications of vulnerability exploitation by embedded shell commands in a user agent and attempts to obtain App Service authentication tokens. articles.title: New investments to reduce on-premises security risk
articles.summary: We’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, bringing together guidance, migration, and product investments. The post New investments to reduce on-premises security risk appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Paul Lorimer
articles.body: On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration, and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now, which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security. Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now. Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation. Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure. This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default. Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain. Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads. On-Premises Baseline Security Mode On-Premises Baseline Security Mode is designed to make the default security posture stronger—reducing the number of recommended security settings administrators must configure and maintain manually. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. Building on protections available today, it progressively establishes and maintains more of the recommended security posture through the products themselves, adapting the baseline as threats and Microsoft security guidance evolve....

articles.author: Alym Rayani
articles.body: Endpoint administrators need to keep elevated access accountable at scale. Security teams also need a clearer view of expert-led protection and a simpler way to deploy SQL Server protection in Azure Government. As AI agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to limit their authority and adapt protection as risk changes. This month’s Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender updates introduce capabilities across these areas, alongside new Secure AI capabilities for agent access. A recent Secure Now update in Microsoft Security Exposure Management also connects information on recent threats to focused initiatives for reducing exposure. Here’s what’s new: Limit agent authority to the task with Dynamic Permissions Give agents task-scoped authority and adapt access as risk changes As agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to manage what each agent is allowed to do. Dynamic Permissions provides an agent its own permissions and authority, scoped to its current task and for only as long as the task requires. As the agent works, Dynamic Agent Risk assesses whether the agent’s authority aligns with changing behavior and context. Dynamic Conditional Access can then respond proportionately by narrowing permissions, restricting access to resources, or requiring human approval for higher-impact actions. Together, these capabilities are designed to help organizations tailor agent authority before an agent acts and adjust access as risk changes. See how security can respond when an agent steps outside its task. Contain local AI agents with Microsoft Execution Containers Apply least-privilege boundaries to help limit access on Windows Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), now generally available, gives organizations an operating system-enforced containment layer for AI agents, designed to limit what an agent can access. Rather than relying on the agent to behave within intended boundaries, MXC applies least-privilege controls across files, networks, processes, and user interactions, with additional isolation options for higher-risk scenarios. Organizations can tune and validate policies before enforcing them broadly, while upcoming integration with Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Agent 365 is intended to extend governance and attribution across the enterprise. articles.body: In this article Spoofed sender domainsQR code phishing attacksCAPTCHA-gated phishing tacticsMalicious payloadsBusiness contact impersonationMicrosoft Teams threatsNotable phishing campaignsDefending against email and collaboration threatsHunting queriesIndicators of compromise (IOCs) Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected approximately 7.3 billion email-based phishing threats from July through September, including a sharp increase to nearly 3 billion in September alone, up 41% from August. Yet the increase did not extend across the techniques that had driven threat actor activity earlier in the year. QR code phishing remained far below its early-year peak, while CAPTCHA-gated phishing reversed several months of decline, driven in part by renewed use of SVG attachments. Q2 in review Shifting tactics and other trends › Figure 1. Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services. Many were delivered because organization- or user-configured exceptions overrode security protections, even after the messages failed authentication checks and were identified as malicious, showing how overly broad exceptions intended to preserve legitimate workflows can also expose them to impersonation. In Microsoft Teams, attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names rather than explicit help desk identities while continuing to use live interactions for social engineering. Across malicious attachment activity more broadly, credential theft remained the dominant objective in Q3. Two campaigns observed during the quarter illustrate the range of activity behind these trends. An August campaign targeting legal organizations used personalized salary review documents and QR codes to lead recipients into device code phishing, despite the broader decline in QR code attacks. In September, purchase order and payroll lures used disguised archives to deliver Agent Tesla, malware commonly used to collect credentials and other information. Together, the campaigns show how familiar business requests remained effective lures across distinct attack paths. articles.summary: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As...
articles.author: CISA
articles.body: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

articles.body: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). articles.body: Published: 2026-11-04Description Description Severity Notes A vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was discovered in the Linux kernel IPv4 TCP stack. The flaw can cause a kernel panic or a container escape (root code execution on the node). An unprivileged process in a container can trigger it locally, without special capabilities such as CAP_NET_RAW. A network attacker can also trigger it by sending TCP packets with IPv4 options to a listener on the node or on the cluster control plane. The network attack requires access to a TCP listener on your nodes, Pods, or the control plane's IP-based endpoint. Clusters that restrict this access to trusted sources, for example with firewall rules and control plane authorized networks, are not exposed to network attacks. GKE Standard clusters and GKE Autopilot clusters are impacted. For instructions and more details, see the GKE security bulletin. Medium CVE-2026-98432

Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked. Google Cloud infrastructure has not been breached. Security telemetry shows no evidence of exploitation against Google Cloud workloads. Applications built with the Google Cloud SDK Libraries are affected if their TLS trust store still accepts emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3, or AAA Certificate Services. The Google Cloud SDK Libraries themselves don't bundle CA certificates, with one exception: Java's com.google.api-client:google-api-client before 2.9.2. In all other cases, the trust store comes from a transport dependency (including the Google-maintained gRPC packages), the language runtime, or the operating system, so the fix is an update to those rather than to the Google Cloud SDK Libraries. In Java, Ruby, and PHP, upgrading the Google client libraries also pulls the fix in. The sections below give the action for each language. What should I do? Find your language below and apply the recommended actions. Then rebuild and redeploy your container images. You can take the following actions to resolve these issues: Upgrade certifi to 2026.10.19 or later. Upgrade httplib2 to 0.32.1 or later. Upgrade grpcio to 1.84.1 or later. Patch releases for earlier release lines are being published; see GHSA-2xm2-c8xx-p9vh for the current list of fixed versions. Advisories: GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2 (certifi), GHSA-2xm2-c8xx-p9vh (grpcio). articles.body: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website. Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. About the vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619- RCE via stale global state Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The vulnerabilities relate to PHP handling of memory when a request terminates abnormally, for example due to memory exhaustion or a fatal error. Under certain conditions, improper memory handling could allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution. Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. Refer to vendor guidancefor patching of different versions of PHP. Recommended action: upgrade PHP We recommend that customers: Upgrade all PHP deployments to a patched version, including virtual machines, containers, base images, and platform runtimes. We suggest prioritizing internet-facing workloads. Rebuild and redeploy container images that include their own PHP runtime, since updating the host does not update PHP inside an image. Migrate to a supported PHP branch if the branch currently in use no longer receives security fixes. Treat the Azure WAF mitigations below as a temporary, supplementary measure. They address a specific technique and do not remediate the underlying vulnerabilities. articles.body: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-27834 Apple Multiple Products Improper Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.body: In this article Attack chain overviewMitigation and protection guidanceLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam
articles.body: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscapeVulnerabilities exploited in the wildWhere defenders should focusPatching is slow, while exploitation is fastImpact, exposure and where to focusNext in lineHow Microsoft Security helps defenders actReferencesLearn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data...

articles.author: yuvalpery
articles.body: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (Brotli releases). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (Node.js security release). If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. Built-in protection enabled by default If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2 on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against crafted Brotli-compressed request bodies. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict the Content-Encoding header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. If your application uses Next.js image optimization, apply the BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 custom rule below, even if you're on DRS 2.2. Custom rules to mitigate CVE-2026-111497 The custom rules block two attack vectors: 1. CVE2026111497 blocks any request whose Content-Encoding header includes the br (Brotli) coding, which this attack uses. DRS 2.2 already covers this vector through rule 920450. articles.author: MaximeBombardier
articles.body: In April, I published a set of referential architecture diagrams for Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Purview Referential Architecture Diagrams. They have been useful in workshops and training sessions for a simple reason: one picture is worth a thousand words - attempting to explain the complex in a single image. Today I'm publishing an update focused on classification and labeling — and on the wave of public previews that make auto-labeling something you can scale across the entire estate with ease. ➡️ Download the interactive architecture on GitHub here. It's a self-contained HTML file - and it's a lot more than this picture! Why now: auto-labeling scales to the whole estate The most consequential change is surprisingly small. An auto-labeling policy can now be kept on while you edit it, without re-triggering simulation. Anyone who has run auto-labeling at scale knows why that matters. Until now, tuning a policy meant turning enforcement off, re-simulating, waiting, and turning it back on — delays every time you refined a rule. That friction made it challenging for organizations from broadening scope as fast as they wanted to. Removing it changes the operating model: you can simulate once with your conditions and expand scope (sites) when you're ready, without hitting the simulation limit. It arrives alongside a set of previews that lift every ceiling that used to cap the motion: Capacity is up 5x. Auto-labeling for SharePoint and OneDrive moves from 100,000 to up to 500,000 files per tenant per day (Roadmap ID 567890). Simulation goes from 4M to 20M items, so you can model against a real estate rather than a sample. Policy scope gets much bigger. Select up to 1,000 individual SharePoint sites per policy, adaptive scopes support up to 50,000 sites, and you can filter sites by the SiteTemplate property when configuring a policy (Roadmap ID 570445, MC1469958). A per-policy coverage report correlates files processed during enforcement to the latest simulation run — including the files that enforcement processed but simulation never saw (Roadmap ID 568935). articles.summary: Teams support impersonation led to remote access, malicious runtime execution, and Certificate Services abuse through authentication relay and Kerberos. The post From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Sagar Patil, Jesse Birch and Tal Tzhori
articles.body: In this article Activity overviewAttack chain overviewPortable runtime staging and execution variantsHost discovery and AD CS assessmentCase 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusionCase 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identityWhy the response outcomes differedActionable investigation methodsReferencesLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths. Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication). This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations. On eligible, onboarded devices, Defender discovers supported agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to give security teams visibility for their local agent environment. Teams can deploy runtime protection at scale from either the Microsoft Defender portal or the Microsoft Intune portal, with Intune-based deployment available in preview. articles.author: tejaskashyap
articles.body: Linux supports cloud services, containers, developer environments, business-critical applications, and a growing share of AI infrastructure. That makes Linux both essential to modern enterprises and increasingly attractive to attackers. AI is compressing the time required to research targets, vary payloads, and adapt when an attempt fails. Customers need protection that can recognize modern attacker behavior at runtime, continuously test effectiveness against realistic attacks, and learn and evolve with the threat landscape. That’s why Microsoft Defender is focused on three priorities for Linux: stronger runtime protection for fileless and in-memory attacks, continuous validation that proves protection remains effective, and AI-powered defense that can help security teams simulate attacks, investigate threats, close protection gaps, and reduce exploitable paths before compromise. A new Linux threat model The threat landscape has evolved from AI-assisted attacks, where people use AI to accelerate individual tasks, to AI-operated attacks, where AI coordinates more of the attack chain, and now it is moving to autonomous AI attacks that can adapt and act with limited human direction. Modern Linux attacks rarely depend on one file; they combine exposed services, stolen credentials, legitimate administration tools, scripts, containers, and cloud-native attack paths. As AI helps attackers generate and modify payloads at scale, adapt when an attempt fails, and move through the attack chain faster, defenders can no longer assume that every payload, script, or binary will resemble something they have seen before. Microsoft Security Research recently observed compromises involving a LiteLLM gateway, a RAGFlow deployment, and a Kestra workflow environment. The intrusion paths differed, but the objectives converged around credential theft, persistence, downstream access, and compute monetization. The broader lesson is that AI gateways, retrieval platforms, and orchestration services are becoming high-value control points where data, credentials, model connectivity, and workload execution meet. These examples also highlight a broader shift: attackers increasingly abuse legitimate services, tools, and workflows rather than relying solely on overtly malicious binaries. Viewed one event at a time, Bash, Python, curl, SSH, and network connections can appear legitimate. The security challenge is to understand their sequence, process relationships, destinations, and runtime...

articles.author: IustinIrimia
articles.body: Attacks rarely stay in one channel. A flood of spam email, a Teams chat from an unfamiliar organization, and a call from "the helpdesk" can all be part of the same attempt. Security teams need a unified way to see where attacks are happening across email and collaboration, investigate them quickly, and show whether their defenses and users are improving. That's the job of our Detections and Insights reports. They're ready-to-use templates that turn Defender's email and collaboration data into views your team can use every day, as a Microsoft Sentinel workbook or a Power BI report. Today we're releasing version 4, which builds on Part 3 of this series, with new hunting queries and a new report for attack simulation training. Shaped by customer feedback, it helps you: See the attacks that matter with new Teams and impersonation views. Investigate faster with 125 new or improved hunting queries. Measure and improve resilience with a new attack simulation training report. See the attacks that matter In September, Microsoft Threat Intelligence described a campaign that starts on Teams: an attacker from another organization poses as IT support in a chat or call and talks the user into a remote session. Spotting activity like this early means looking at Teams alongside email. articles.author: Microsoft
articles.body: Updated October 26, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience. [What and why]Users will soon be able to register a passkey as their first multifactor authentication method. Previously, people had to set up an alternate MFA method like SMS or Voice before they could add a passkey (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO. That extra step pushed users toward weaker methods and slowed the move to phishing-resistant sign-in. Now password-only users can go straight to a passkey, making it easier to adopt strong authentication from day one. As part of this work, we will also be enabling Authenticator App passwordless sign-in to be a user's first registered MFA method. [Rollout schedule]This feature will roll out in phases: Phase 1: Support for synced passkeys, Microsoft Entra passkeys on Windows, and FIDO2 security keys. General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We will begin rolling out in early November 2026 (previously late October) and expect to complete by early January 2027 (previously late November 2026). Phase 2: Support for Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO, Authenticator App passkey, and Authenticator App passwordless sign-in. General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We will begin rolling out in early January 2026 and expect to complete by late February 2027. [Impact on your organization]Who is affectedUsers who have not yet registered a multifactor authentication methodIdentity and security administrators responsible for authentication onboarding and registration policiesPlatforms and servicesMicrosoft Entra IDPasskeys (FIDO2)Windows Hello for BusinessmacOS Platform SSOMicrosoft Authenticator passwordless sign-inWhat will happenPassword-only users will be able to register passkeys or passwordless sign-in as their first MFA method.Users will no longer need to register a method such as SMS or voice before registering a passkey (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO, or Authenticator passwordless sign-in.Organizations may see reduced registration friction and increased adoption of phishing-resistant authentication methods.Users who are enabled for passkeys will be prompted to register a passkey by default when completing applicable registration experiences, including those triggered by multifactor authentication (MFA) enforcement and Conditional Access authentication strengths. Security Defaults MFA registration prompts will adopt this experience in January–February 2027.[Action required and recommendations]No action is required for this change.We recommend that administrators:Review Conditional Access policies related to security information registration.Consider requiring MFA to register security information if additional verification is required by your organization.Review your user onboarding and registration guidance and update it as needed to reflect that eligible users may be prompted to register a passkey by default.Learn more (To be updated closer to rollout) Register a synced passkey (FIDO2) | Authentication | Microsoft Entra ID | Microsoft Learn[Compliance considerations]QuestionAnswerDoes the change include an admin control?Yes. Administrators can control which authentication methods users are allowed to register through existing Microsoft Entra authentication method policies and Conditional Access policies.Does the change affect access or authentication controls?Yes. The update changes how users register multifactor authentication methods by allowing eligible users to register supported passkeys or passwordless authentication methods as their first MFA method.Can administrators govern the feature through existing Microsoft Entra controls?Yes. Administrators retain control over the feature through Microsoft Entra authentication method policies and Conditional Access configurations.

articles.body: Email remains the most exploited gateway for cyberattacks, as the threat landscape continues to get more sophisticated with attackers using AI to scale phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Microsoft Defender is a leading email security solution, helping organizations stay ahead of these threats with a modern, cloud-native approach. At the same time, many organizations choose to layer additional email security solutions to meet compliance requirements or align to an existing defense-in-depth strategy. This approach can strengthen resilience, but it can also add operational complexity for SOC teams. Today, we’re continuing to expand the ICES vendor ecosystem by adding Proofpoint Core Email Protection API. Proofpoint joins existing members Darktrace, KnowBe4, Cisco, and VIPRE Security Group. How joint customers benefit from a streamlined SOC experience in Microsoft Defender The ICES ecosystem brings trusted third-party email security verdicts and telemetry into the Defender portal through an API-based integration model. This allows Microsoft Defender to acknowledge partner verdicts on messages, apply the highest-severity determination, and surface that information in the same investigation and response workflows security teams already use. The integration with Proofpoint Core Email Protection API is designed specifically for customers who have already chosen to deploy Proofpoint’s ICES solution alongside Microsoft Defender. It supports environments where customers run both solutions and want to reduce friction for their SOC teams. By integrating Proofpoint into the ICES ecosystem, customers can now preserve their existing security strategy while improving how investigations and response are carried out day to day. articles.body: Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today. Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program. What employees should know This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below. This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs. Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours. Looking ahead The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute. My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving. Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another. articles.author: JerryDevore
articles.body: Hi all. Jerry Devore dropping in for a minute to share some insights about the BlockNtlmv1SSO setting that went into effect with the October 2026 update. Why the change was necessary When MS-CHAPv2 is used for solutions like VPN, Wi-Fi, NPS, and RADIUS, the authentication flow leverages the MD4 hash of the account’s password to respond to a challenge. If that sounds familiar, then you have at least a basic understanding of NTLM. The problem is that this relic from 1998 (NT 4.0 SP4) produces a response to the challenge that is cryptographically equivalent to NTLMv1. So, while a device using MS-CHAPv2 can have NTLMv1 disabled, it is still exposing the same type of challenge response that makes NTLMv1 trivial to crack. The Change B ack in August 2025, an update added support for the registry setting BlockNtlmv1SSO (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0). The update did not create the registry setting, but it caused devices to start auditing for the use of "NTLMv1-derived credentials". With the October 2026 update, the default for Windows devices is to block the use of NTLMv1-derived credentials. This means that organizations that are still dependent on CHAPv2 are going to be impacted. Bracing for Impact For organizations that have already blocked NTLMv1 in their domains, there is no required action because MS-CHAPv2 using domain credentials is already impossible. For everyone else, you might want to do your due diligence before letting the October update rip if you are not certain whether you have any dependencies on MS-CHAPv2. The documentation for this change mentions events 4024 (Warning) and 4025 (Error) which are logged to the NTLM log of the client (Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational). Those events are extremely helpful, but very few organizations are forwarding the client NTLM logs to their SIEM. Possibly a better approach The October 2026 update giveth and the October update taketh away. What do I mean by that? Besides taking away NTLMv1-derived credentials, the update backported the enhanced NTLM auditing events to Server 2019 and Server 2022. As a result, you can leverage your domain controllers’ logs to determine if you have any MS-CHAPv2 dependencies prior to updating your endpoints. Here is an example of a 4033 event logged on a domain controller when the VPN server forwarded the challenge response for "credential validation". articles.author: Microsoft Security Research and Microsoft Threat Intelligence
articles.body: In this article What’s happeningWhat is ARTEX?Mitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access. This allowed the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access. The activity conducted by the threat actor through the usage of ARTEX framework did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services. Although Microsoft identified Storm-0940-initiated authentication and follow-on activity in multiple customer environments, the presence of an affected application or successful threat actor authentication does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated. articles.body: As security teams bring in more data from more sources and use it across SIEM and XDR workflows, decisions about connector health, ingestion volume, and cost optimization get harder. Today, we’re announcing the public preview of Unified Data Management for Microsoft Sentinel, available in the new Data & connectors experience in the Microsoft Defender portal, so you can monitor and manage your data from a single place. What Unified Data Management is and why it matters Unified Data Management brings connectors, tables, and ingestion health together. Instead of moving between separate pages, you can see your full data landscape, spot issues, and act on them from one view. It’s designed to help you quickly answer questions like: Which connectors are configured and which need attention? Which tables are receiving data? Are there ingestion spikes, drops, or stale data patterns? Which tables drive the most ingestion volume? What schema, transformations, and retention settings apply to a table? You’ll find it under Setup & configuration > Data & connectors, organized into three tabs: Overview, Connectors, and Tables. Overview: See health at a glance The Overview tab gives you a workspace-level snapshot of ingestion and health, so you can catch data issues before they impact analytics, detections, investigations, or reporting. It surfaces: Ingestion volume: Daily ingestion split by Analytics tier and Data Lake tier for your selected time range. Connectors that need attention: Connectors with credential errors, ingestion failures, or outages, including error type, failure count, and last successful ingestion. Table ingestion fluctuations: Tables with unexpected volume changes, grouped into spikes and drops. Data ingestion volume by table: Your top ingesting tables, ranked by daily volume. Ingestion latency by table: How long it takes for data to become available after it’s generated. Together, these insights help you troubleshoot connector failures, track down cost spikes, validate that new connectors are flowing, and catch unexpected changes in volume. What changes are what customers see: one unit and one price. Workload-specific usage is converted into DWUs and aggregated across your environment, based on a consistent global per-unit price calculated hourly and billed monthly. Estimation, reporting, and billing use the same DWU framework, making it easier to understand how usage translates into cost. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. YouTube Video Click here to load media A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. articles.author: Hayete Gallot
articles.body: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful. While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents. Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised. Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise. They are agentic insiders. Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly. To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7. An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime. In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise. articles.body: By: Christian Friedel-Jain - Sr. Security Consultant | James Noyce - Sr. Security Solution Engineer Introduction Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) are among the most sensitive endpoints in any organization. A PAW, in most of our Microsoft consulting projects, exists to do one job safely: administer cloud services from a hardened device that is only ever allowed to reach a small, tightly controlled set of internet destinations. But an endpoint’s security posture is ultimately defined by its behavior under failure conditions. When we moved the internet access restriction for our PAW devices from a locally enforced restriction (more about that later) to a solution based on Microsoft Global Secure Access (GSA), we immediately identified a gap under failure conditions – but first a quick grounding on the moving parts. Global Secure Access (What is Global Secure Access?) is Microsoft’s umbrella term for Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access — the components of Microsoft’s Security Service Edge solution. For a PAW device we are leveraging Microsoft Entra Internet Access as an identity centric secure web gateway solution to control exactly which internet destinations the workstation can reach, by applying a fine-grained set of rules and policies enforced through Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra. This configuration provides us better filtering capabilities, like web content filtering (Global Secure Access web content filtering) with TLS inspection (TLSi) (Global Secure Access transport layer security inspection) and additional features like Threat Intelligence (Global Secure Access threat intelligence), but it comes also with a downside. Currently by default, if the GSA client encounters an issue or cannot connect to its required GSA edge services, the GSA client will fall back to a fail-open state, rather than to a fail-close state. Difference between those two modes: Fail-Open: When a security or control mechanism fails, access is still allowed. Fail-Close: When the security or control mechanism fails, access is blocked. This blog post covers above problem and showcases a solution we built, as part of our projects, to achieve a “Fail-Close” state rather than having the current “Fail-Open” behavior. articles.summary: Potentially Unwanted Applications, or PUA, they aren't necessarily malware, but they are applications you probably don't want running across your environment either. Microsoft defines potentially unwanted applications as software that can adversely affect endpoint performance or use. Examples...
articles.author: Vytas_Boyev
articles.body: Potentially Unwanted Applications, or PUA, they aren't necessarily malware, but they are applications you probably don't want running across your environment either. Microsoft defines potentially unwanted applications as software that can adversely affect endpoint performance or use. Examples include advertising software, software bundlers, and applications that use behaviors intended to evade security products. Microsoft Defender can also consider an application's reputation when determining whether software qualifies as potentially unwanted. That sounds straightforward. On Windows, it generally is. On Linux, finding the resulting audit events requires knowing exactly where to look. And that is where things get interesting. PUA, PUP… Same Neighborhood, Slightly Different Address Before going further, it is worth clearing up some terminology. Across the security industry, you will commonly encounter both PUP, or Potentially Unwanted Program, and PUA, or Potentially Unwanted Application. The terms are frequently used for software that isn't necessarily malicious but has characteristics that make its presence undesirable, such as intrusive advertising, bundling additional software, or other behavior the user might not have knowingly requested. Microsoft uses Potentially Unwanted Application (PUA) as its product and detection terminology. Microsoft specifically distinguishes PUA from malware. A PUA might cause poor system performance, display unexpected advertisements, install other software, or have a poor reputation because of undesirable behavior, but those characteristics don't automatically make the application malware. Microsoft's classification criteria include examples such as: Advertising software that displays advertisements or promotions, including injecting advertisements into webpages. Bundling software that offers to install additional software that isn't digitally signed by the same entity, or that itself qualifies as PUA. Evasion software that actively attempts to avoid detection by security products or behaves differently when security software is present. Applications that have developed a poor reputation based on undesirable behavior. Microsoft's broader software-classification model also distinguishes between unknown software, malware, unwanted software, and other classifications. Software can therefore be legitimate and functional while still meeting Microsoft's criteria for classification as potentially unwanted. For the rest of this...

articles.body: Updated October 8, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience.[What and why]Microsoft Entra ID will support passkey registration and sign-in for B2B users, including internal guest users and external users. Eligible B2B users will be able to register and use passkeys issued by the resource tenant to satisfy that tenant's multifactor authentication (MFA) requirements.Passkeys are already supported for member users in their home tenant. Until now, B2B users could not use a resource tenant passkey when that tenant required MFA and did not trust the home tenant's MFA. This update closes that gap and gives guest and external users a phishing-resistant way to satisfy MFA requirements in the resource tenant.B2B users can register a resource tenant passkey from the resource tenant's My Security Info page, during a proof-up prompt, or through a passkey registration campaign. Once registered, the passkey can satisfy the resource tenant's MFA requirements during sign-in.Microsoft Authenticator app passkeys will be supported for internal guest users but not for external users.Important: This rollout intersects with the previously announced retirement of SMS and voice authentication. As described in Message Center posts MC1426371 and MC1434201, any user enabled for SMS or voice in the Authentication methods policy or legacy MFA policies will be automatically enabled for all passkey types. This will include eligible B2B users when B2B passkey support becomes available.[Rollout schedule]General Availability (GCC, Worldwide): Beginning in late October 2026, with a phased rollout as outlined below:Internal guest users: Beginning in late October 2026 (previously early October) and is expected to complete by late November 2026 (previously late October)External users (excluding Microsoft Authenticator app passkeys): Rollout timing will be communicated in a future Message center post update.[Impact on your organization]Who is affectedMicrosoft Entra administrators managing Authentication methods policiesOrganizations that use Microsoft Entra B2B collaborationInternal guest users and external users who are in scope for passkey authenticationInternal guest users and external users who are enabled for SMS or voice in the Authentication methods policy or legacy MFA policiesPlatforms and servicesMicrosoft Entra IDMy Security InfoAuthentication methods policyConditional AccessWhat will happenThe feature will be enabled by default.B2B users who are already in scope for passkeys in your Authentication methods policy will automatically be able to register and sign in with resource tenant passkeys.Eligible B2B users may receive prompts to register a passkey during sign-in through proof-up experiences or passkey registration campaigns, if those experiences are configured in your tenant.Users can also register a passkey from the resource tenant's My Security Info page.If your organization has excluded B2B users from passkeys in the Authentication methods policy, and those users are not separately subject to automatic passkey enablement through the SMS and voice retirement changes, they will not be prompted and will not be able to register or sign in with a resource tenant passkey.Under the SMS and voice retirement changes described in MC1426371 and MC1434201, B2B users who are enabled for SMS or voice in the Authentication methods policy or legacy MFA policies will be automatically enabled for all passkey types. Excluding these users from the passkey policy alone will not prevent this automatic enablement if they remain enabled for SMS or voice.This change gives guest and external users a phishing-resistant sign-in option and helps organizations extend strong authentication requirements to their B2B population.[Action required and recommendations]No action is required.We recommend that administrators review current passkey and MFA configurations before rollout:Review your Authentication methods policy. Confirm which users are in scope for passkeys, including guest and external users. B2B users who are in scope will be enabled automatically. Exclude them from the policy if that is not the intended behavior.Review Message Center posts MC1426371 and MC1434201 for details about the SMS and voice retirement changes.Review SMS and voice assignments in both the Authentication methods policy and legacy MFA policies. If you do not want specific B2B users to be automatically enabled for all passkey types, move those users off SMS and voice in all applicable policies. Excluding them only from the passkey policy is not sufficient while they remain enabled for SMS or voice.Review your passkey registration campaign. Confirm that the campaign's user scope includes the intended users.Review your Conditional Access policies. Confirm that MFA and authentication strength requirements will apply as intended for B2B users when resource tenant passkeys become available.Confirm user scoping across authentication-related policies. Make sure the groups and user types targeted by each policy align with your organization's requirements for guest and external users.Consider notifying your help desk and identity support teams that eligible B2B users may begin receiving passkey registration prompts after rollout.[Compliance considerations]QuestionAnswerDoes the change store new customer data?Passkey credential registration data may be stored as part of Microsoft Entra authentication management.Does the change alter how existing customer data is processed, stored, or accessed?The change introduces an additional authentication method for B2B users accessing resource tenant resources.

articles.body: Email remains one of the most common entry points for security threats. Yet email products often describe the same activity with different table names, fields, and values. This makes it harder to build detections and investigations that work consistently across data sources. The Microsoft Sentinel Advanced Security Information Model, or ASIM, EmailEvent schema is now available. It provides a common structure for email delivery and inspection events, helping customers and partners create security content that works across supported email data sources. A consistent view of email security activity EmailEvent standardizes the information analysts need to understand what happened to an email and why. It covers: Email delivery and inspection events Sender, source, and recipient information Message subject, size, direction, and delivery location URLs and file attachments SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication results Delivery actions such as delivered, blocked, quarantined, or deleted Threat, risk, confidence, tactic, technique, and remediation details Instead of learning a different data model for every product, analysts can query the normalized EmailEvent fields. Parser developers map each source's native data to the same schema. How it works Consider an email that contains a suspicious attachment. The email security product records the sender, recipients, attachment, authentication results, inspection verdict, and final action. A connector collects that event. A parser or Data Collection Rule maps the source fields to EmailEvent. Microsoft Sentinel can then query the normalized record using the same field names used for other supported email sources. This common structure separates security content from the details of a specific product. When another source adds an EmailEvent parser, existing source-independent queries and detections can work with that source without being rewritten around its native field names. Why it matters Simpler analytics: Write queries against one consistent set of email fields. Broader coverage: Apply source-independent security content across normalized email sources. Faster investigations: Compare delivery, authentication, attachment, URL, and threat details without translating different data models. Easier integration: Give connector and parser developers a defined contract for bringing new email telemetry into ASIM.
